A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same diffusion Thompson sampling work. Their text, equations, figures, tables and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison despite extensive reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-bandit simulations, algorithm comparisons and parameter-scaling experiments in Section 5 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 reports original synthetic, Swiss-roll, MovieLens and CIFAR-10 experiments, including robustness and posterior-approximation evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix G.

M1.justification: Remark 3.1 explicitly formulates a shared-parameter variant using action-dependent features, which Appendix G.4 applies to CIFAR-10; v1 only discusses this alternative setting when explaining dependence on K. The main hierarchical sampler, Gaussian likelihood approximation and nonlinear-link approximation remain substantively unchanged.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates only diffusion-generated synthetic bandits. v2 adds Swiss-roll action distributions, semi-synthetic MovieLens recommendations, CIFAR-10 classification-derived bandits and mismatched-prior scenarios. Appendix G.4 also states that similar MNIST results were obtained, without displaying them.

E2.justification: The synthetic comparisons retain LinUCB, LinTS, HierTS, UCB-GLM and GLM-TS in their corresponding settings. v2 adds targeted comparisons against MCMC-Fast and MCMC-Slow on MovieLens (Table 2), plus an exact Gaussian posterior reference for approximation validation (Figure 5).

E3.justification: The main synthetic comparison adds the configuration d=5, K=100, L=2, and nonlinear-diffusion plots extend from 1,000 to 5,000 rounds. New protocols vary prior perturbations, pretraining sample sizes from 10 to 50,000, diffusion depth from 2 to 100 and CIFAR-10 offline-data fractions. v2 also introduces regret ratios, percentage improvements and timing comparisons.

E4.justification: Existing action-count, dimension, depth and reward-misspecification analyses are retained. v2 adds prior-perturbation robustness, pretraining-data and depth sensitivity, CIFAR-10 offline-data ablations, learned-distribution visualizations, posterior-quality checks against exact inference and MCMC, and numerical comparisons of regret bounds (Figures 2c–6 and Appendix G).

E5.justification: Both experimental sections specify 50 random simulations and average regret with standard errors. No changed run count, seed policy, confidence-interval procedure or significance-testing practice is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results for new configurations, datasets and analyses. Table 2 reports dTS regret improvements of 50.6% against MCMC-Fast and 12.7% against MCMC-Slow. Table 3 reports CIFAR-10 improvements with 1% offline data of 69.11% against HierTS and 87.74% against LinTS. These are newly reported comparisons, not same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: The main regret theorem, sparsity proposition and regret proofs survive as Theorem E.1, Proposition E.2 and Appendix F. However, v1 Appendix B's detailed action- and latent-posterior proofs, including Lemma B.3, are omitted. v2 retains the update formulas and refers their derivation to earlier work, removing a substantial self-contained mathematical component.

C1.justification: The central claim that diffusion priors enable efficient contextual Thompson sampling, supported by exact linear-case inference and regret analysis, remains. v2 adds broader contribution claims for diffusion-prior posterior inference beyond bandits and presents dTS as online diffusion fine-tuning from implicit feedback (Introduction and Conclusion).

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive applicability limits concerning scarce or biased offline data, unstructured or purely online regimes, and unquantified approximation errors. It explicitly acknowledges that the linear-Gaussian theoretical setting does not require diffusion models. New interpretations explain the pretraining-depth tradeoff and the approximate posterior's retained diffusion structure (Sections 3.2–5.2 and Appendices D and H).

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link and a pretraining recipe specifying JAX, a two-layer ReLU network, noise-prediction loss, Adam with learning rate 0.001, 20,000 epochs and batch size min(2048, sample size). It also describes MovieLens embedding construction and reports 30-CPU hardware (Appendices G.2 and J). These disclosures go substantially beyond v1's synthetic-generator settings.

R1.justification: v2 adds relevant references including Kveton et al.'s diffusion-prior posterior sampling, diffusion inference, lower bounds and offline learning. It more explicitly attributes the fully linear precursor to Aouali (2023), previously mentioned as a preliminary workshop version. Most of Appendix A's positioning relative to hierarchical and structured bandits remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, method exposition and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. The four linear/nonlinear method cases become a consolidated posterior-approximation presentation; formal theory moves to appendices while informal insights remain in the main text. Terminology and notation are revised, and the appendices are substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column main text to a single-column layout. The graphical-model diagram is removed; v1 Figures 2 and 4 become an expanded comparison grid, while Figures 3 and 5 reappear as v2 Figures 2a and 2b. New empirical plots, distribution visualizations, a notation table and two result tables substantially change the presentation.

improvement.justification: Section 5.2 and Appendix G substantially address v1's main evidential gap: practical effectiveness was supported only on diffusion-generated synthetic problems. Learned-prior evaluations, robustness checks and approximation comparisons provide broader support, while implementation details and explicit applicability limits improve transparency. These gains outweigh reduced self-containment from omitted posterior proofs, although some new benchmark and MCMC settings remain sparsely documented.
